Delphi. Nestled high in the slopes of Mount Parnassus in central Greece, it was the sacred heart of the Greek world and home to the most renowned oracle in antiquity. Kings, generals, and common folk journeyed to the Temple of Apollo to consult the Pythia, the priestess who delivered cryptic prophecies that shaped the course of Greek history.

Delphi was built as a sanctuary to Apollo after he slew the serpent Python, establishing a pilgrimage site of unparalleled religious authority across the entire Greek world. The Oracle of Delphi spoke through the Pythia, a priestess in ecstatic trance, who delivered prophecies in verse. These prophecies were cryptic and often doubled-edged, meaning they could be interpreted in multiple ways.

Above the temple entrance were inscribed two axioms that became foundational to Greek philosophy and ethics: "Know thyself" and "Nothing in excess." Delphi hosted the Pythian Games, celebrated every four years, which were second only to the Olympic Games in prestige. The games featured athletic contests and musical competitions that drew competitors from across the Greek world.

Delphi served as a pan-Hellenic sanctuary where Greeks of all city-states gathered, transcending their political rivalries and reinforcing the cultural unity of the Greek people. The sanctuary housed the Omphalos, or navel of the world—a conical stone that marked the center of the earth in Greek cosmology. The oracle's influence declined with the rise of Christianity. The sanctuary was closed by Roman emperors, and the Pythia's final prophecy was recorded in the fourth century CE.

Apollo was the god whose oracle the sanctuary honored. The serpent Python had been slain by Apollo, and that slaying sanctified the site itself. The Amphictyonic League, a religious confederation, managed Delphi and the Pythian Games. Delphi rivaled the Olympics as another pan-Hellenic sanctuary of supreme importance to the Greek world.
